why:
The Caro-Kann is a solid answer to 1.e4. You play 1...c6 and then 2...d5. The c6 pawn guards the d5 pawn, so your centre pawn has support from the start.

In most lines your light-squared bishop comes out to f5 or g4 before you play ...e6. After that, ...e6 does not shut the bishop in behind your pawns. The Panov is the exception: there the bishop stays at home for a while.

The opening asks for patience. In the Advance Variation White has more space, and you must wait for your moment. Your main pawn break is ...c5. In some lines you also play ...e5.

The Slav, your answer to 1.d4, uses the same ideas. It has a pawn on c6 that supports d5. In many Slav lines the light-squared bishop comes out before ...e6.

variations.middlegame:
Finish your development with ...Ngf6, ...e6, ...Be7 and ...O-O. The order can change. A typical move order is h5 Bh7 Bd3 Bxd3 Qxd3 e6 Bf4 Ngf6 O-O-O Be7 Kb1 O-O.

When your pieces are out, play the pawn break ...c5. It hits the d4 pawn.

mistakes.text: White plays h5 and attacks your bishop. Move the bishop at once with ...Bh7. If you play another move, such as ...e6, White takes it with hxg6.
Playing ...e6 before ...Bf5 shuts the bishop in. On c8 it has only the d7 square. Play ...Bf5 first.

variations.middlegame:
Your plan is to hit the base of the white pawn chain. The ...c5 break does this. After ...cxd4 and Nxd4 the chain is broken. The e5 pawn has no pawn behind it.

Next you play ...Nbc6 to attack the knight on d4. Your e7 knight can go to g6 and attack the e5 pawn. Castle short when your pieces are out.

mistakes.text: Playing ...e6 before ...Bf5 shuts the bishop in. On c8 it has only the d7 square. The position is not lost, but you give up the main idea of the Caro-Kann. Play ...Bf5 first.
Do not play ...Nf6 here. The e5 pawn takes it with exf6, and you lose a knight for a pawn. Play ...e6.
Do not take the pawn with ...Bxg4. White plays Qxg4, because the queen on d1 sees g4. You lose a bishop for a pawn. Play ...Bg6.

variations.middlegame:
In the Panov White often gets an isolated pawn on d4. It has no pawn on the c-file or the e-file. A knight on d5 stands in front of it and blocks it. Trade pieces and attack the d4 pawn with ...Nc6.

A typical plan is ...Nc6 and ...O-O. Your knight is already on f6.

mistakes.text: This is off the route: you played ...Nc6 and ...Bg4 instead of ...e6. The queen on b3 attacks the b7 pawn and your d5 knight. The c3 knight also attacks d5. Do not play ...e6. Then Qxb7 attacks your c6 knight and your a8 rook. Play ...Bxf3 first. It removes the guard of d4. After gxf3 e6 Qxb7, take the pawn with ...Nxd4.

Develop ...Nf6, which hits the e4 pawn. Then play ...Nbd7, ...Bc5 or ...Be7, and castle short. A typical order is d3 Nf6 Be2 Nbd7 O-O Bc5 Bf4 O-O.

Keep the d5 pawn guarded at all times. The e4 pawn and the c3 knight both attack it, and the queen on f3 stands behind the e4 pawn.
